specPoints.text: describe patterns of monohybrid inheritance using a genetic diagram
predict probabilities of outcomes from monohybrid crosses

primer.text: One gene, one square grid, and the whole pattern of inheritance becomes predictable. This note builds the Punnett square step by step, runs the classic pea-height crosses — pure breeding, F2 interbreed, and the test cross against a short plant — and converts the familiar 3:1 ratio into percentages you can quote as probabilities.

lessons.title: Building the Square
lessons.opening: A monohybrid cross follows one gene through a generation, and the Punnett square is the tool: place the parental alleles around the grid, fill the four inner cells, and read off every genotype the offspring could carry, with its ratio.
keyPoints: Monohybrid inheritance concerns a characteristic controlled by a single gene.
Parental genotypes are written before any square is drawn.
Choose letters whose capital and lowercase forms look clearly different.
Parental alleles sit on the edges, and the four inner cells list the offspring possibilities.
The grid supports ratios, percentage chances and phenotype predictions.

low.restatement: Write the parents, split their alleles, fill four boxes, count the outcomes.
low.analogy: A two-by-two table pairing one item from each parent, like matching socks from two drawers.
low.examPointer: Avoid lookalike letters such as Cc or Ss when choosing symbols.

medium.restatement: Each parent contributes one allele per gamete, so the grid enumerates every fertilisation outcome exactly once.
medium.analogy: Four doors, each opened by one key from each of two key rings.
medium.examPointer: Comment on ratio, percentage or phenotype exactly as the command word asks.

check.stem: What does monohybrid mean?

options.text: Inheritance of a characteristic controlled by one gene
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Two genes would be a dihybrid case.
Many genes describe polygenic inheritance.
The unit here is one gene, not a chromosome.

check.stem: Which letter pair suits a Punnett square best?

options.text: Bb, because the capital and lowercase forms are clearly different
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Cc, its lowercase form too closely mirrors the capital
options.explanation: Lookalike letters cause marking errors.

options.text: Ss, the same mirror problem applies
options.explanation: S and s are notoriously confusable.

options.text: Two different letters, B and d
options.explanation: The same letter must be used, differing only in case.

check.stem: What fills the four inner cells of the square?

options.text: Every allele combination the offspring could inherit
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The cells hold offspring genotypes.
Mutation plays no role in the grid.
Cells hold allele pairs, not chromosome numbers.

check.stem: A student wants the ratio of phenotypes among offspring. Where does it come from?

options.text: From counting the genotype combinations in the filled grid
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Sizes are irrelevant; the grid is the source.
The ratio falls out of the cell counts.
Each cross needs its own count.

check.stem: Why write the parental genotypes first?

options.text: The square splits whatever alleles the parents actually carry, so an error there ruins every cell
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The reason is genetic, not cosmetic.
Parental genotypes are fixed.

options.text: Because the grid ignores the parents
options.explanation: The grid is built entirely from them.

check.stem: List the steps for building a Punnett square.
check.modelAnswer: Write the parental genotypes, split their alleles around the grid edges, fill the four inner cells, and read the offspring combinations.

check.stem: State what a Punnett square shows.
check.modelAnswer: It shows the possible allele combinations the offspring could receive, from which ratios and probabilities follow.

check.stem: Explain why the square predicts probabilities rather than guarantees.
check.modelAnswer: Each fertilisation is random, so the grid gives the chance of each outcome per pregnancy, not a promise about any particular child.

check.stem: A breeder crosses two rabbits both known to be heterozygous for a single coat-colour gene. Describe how you would lay out the diagram before any mating happens.
check.modelAnswer: Write both parental genotypes as heterozygous pairs, split the alleles around the grid edges, fill the four inner cells with the offspring combinations, and count the resulting ratio.

lessons.title: First Cross: Pure-Breeding Peas
sourceHeadings: Example of monohybrid inheritance: Pea plants
A short plant is bred with a tall plant
lessons.opening: Pea height runs on one gene with two alleles: tall dominates, written T, and short recedes, written t, so crossing a pure-breeding short plant with a pure-breeding tall plant hands every offspring one of each allele.
keyPoints: Pea height is controlled by a single gene with tall and short alleles.
The tall allele T is dominant and the short allele t is recessive.
A pure-breeding short plant is tt and a pure-breeding tall plant is TT.
Every F1 offspring from this cross receives genotype Tt and grows tall.

low.restatement: Short times tall gives all tall offspring, because every seed gets a dominant T.
low.analogy: Two pure recipes blended once: every dish carries both flavours, and the strong one leads.
low.examPointer: State the F1 genotypes as all Tt before saying anything about phenotypes.

medium.restatement: Pure breeding means homozygous, so each parent can pass only one allele type, making the whole F1 uniform.
medium.analogy: Two queues, each handing out one kind of ticket: every pair bought is identical.
medium.examPointer: Explain uniformity through gametes, not through luck.

check.stem: What genotypes do pure-breeding parents carry?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That describes mixed parents, not pure breeding.
That would make both parents short.
The second parent is not pure-breeding.

check.stem: What is the phenotype of every F1 plant from the tt crossed with TT cross?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Each offspring carries the dominant T.
No segregation appears in the F1 here.
That ratio belongs to the F2, not the F1.

check.stem: Why does the tt parent contribute only t alleles?

options.text: A homozygous recessive plant can pass on nothing else
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Plants have no preference.
A tt plant never had a T allele.
Soil does not rewrite alleles.

check.stem: Which allele does the F1 plant's phenotype express?

options.text: The dominant T, while the t stays hidden
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The recessive t, since it came from one parent
options.explanation: Dominance decides expression, not origin.
One of them always expresses.
Only the dominant shows in the phenotype.

check.stem: What ratio appears among the F1 offspring of this cross?

options.text: All tall, so no ratio is needed
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That is the F2 ratio, not the F1.
Uniformity, not a split, marks this cross.
That belongs to dihybrid patterns.

check.stem: Show the F1 result of crossing tt with TT in words.
check.modelAnswer: Every offspring receives T from one parent and t from the other, so all F1 plants are the tall heterozygotes Tt.

check.stem: State which allele is dominant in pea height.
check.modelAnswer: The tall allele T is dominant over the recessive short allele t.

check.stem: Explain why no short plants appear in the F1 generation.
check.modelAnswer: Every F1 plant inherits the dominant T from the tall parent, so the recessive t cannot express itself in any of them.

check.stem: A farmer buys seed from a pure-breeding short strain and a pure-breeding tall strain. Predict the appearance of the entire first crop grown from crossing them.
check.modelAnswer: Every first-generation plant receives one tall and one short allele, so the whole crop grows tall with no short plants appearing.

lessons.title: Second Cross: the F2 Ratio
sourceHeadings: Crossing the offspring from the first cross
lessons.opening: Interbreeding the Tt offspring of the first cross opens the second act: their alleles split evenly in the gametes, so the grid fills with TT, Tt and tt in the familiar one-two-one pattern, read as three tall to every one short.
keyPoints: Each Tt parent produces T and t gametes in equal numbers.
The grid yields TT, Tt and tt genotypes in a 1:2:1 count.
Grouped by phenotype the ratio is three tall to one short.
The F2 generation is what this second cross produces.

low.restatement: Tall times tall now gives three tall and one short among every four offspring.
low.analogy: Two coin-tossers meeting: three of the four pairings look tall, one looks short.
low.examPointer: Quote the ratio as 3:1 and the genotype count as 1:2:1.

medium.restatement: Equal gamete production plus random pairing makes the 1:2:1 genotype pattern, and dominance compresses it visually to 3:1.
medium.analogy: Two lottery drums, each holding equal tickets; the draw table fills predictably.
medium.examPointer: The F2 is where the recessive trait resurfaces; say so explicitly.

check.stem: What genotypes fill the F2 grid from Tt crossed with Tt?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The heterozygous class appears twice.
Uniformity ended with the F1.
That count double-counts the wrong cells.

check.stem: How many of the four cells hold a heterozygous genotype?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Tt occupies two diagonal cells.
Only two cells are mixed.
TT and tt are homozygous.

check.stem: What phenotype ratio marks the F2 generation here?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The recessive form returns in the F2.
That ratio belongs to the test cross.
That belongs to dihybrid patterns.

check.stem: Which genotype guarantees a short plant?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That is the tall homozygote.
The dominant allele masks the short form.

options.text: Any mix of the two letters
options.explanation: Presence of T decides tallness.

check.stem: An F2 short plant is bred on. What is its genotype, and why are you sure?

options.text: tt, because shortness requires two recessive alleles
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
A Tt plant is tall.
Tallness never skips through tt.
Neither carries two recessive copies.

check.stem: Derive the 3:1 ratio from the Tt by Tt grid.
check.modelAnswer: The grid gives one TT, two Tt and one tt, and since Tt plants are tall, three cells are tall to every one short cell.

check.stem: Name the generation produced by interbreeding the F1 plants.
check.modelAnswer: It is called the F2 generation.

check.stem: Explain why the recessive characteristic resurfaces in the F2 after hiding in the F1.
check.modelAnswer: The F1 plants each carry a hidden t allele, so when two of them breed, some offspring receive t from both parents and express the recessive short form.

check.stem: A seed merchant allows the tall F1 plants from the first cross to self-fertilise freely. Predict the ratio of heights among the resulting F2 seedlings.
check.modelAnswer: The F2 seedlings show three tall to every one short, following the 1:2:1 genotype pattern with the dominant phenotype on top.

lessons.title: The Test Cross Against a Short Plant
sourceHeadings: Crossing a heterozygous plant with a short plant
lessons.opening: Pairing a heterozygous tall plant with a genuine short plant changes the odds: the short parent can donate only t, so half the grid fills with Tt tall offspring and half with tt short offspring.
keyPoints: The heterozygous parent is Tt and the short parent must be tt.
Gametes from the first parent carry T or t in equal share.
Gametes from the short parent carry t only.
The grid therefore splits one-to-one between tall and short offspring.

low.restatement: Tall mixed with short gives half tall and half short offspring.
low.analogy: One shuffled deck against a deck of identical cards: half the pairs differ, half match.
low.examPointer: The short parent's genotype is tt, always, in this cross.

medium.restatement: Because one parent offers a single allele type, the cross exposes the hidden allele of the other parent, which is why it is called a test cross.
medium.analogy: A lie-detector for genotype: the uniform partner reveals whatever the tested parent hides.
medium.examPointer: If a tall plant crossed with a short one yields short offspring, the tall parent must be Tt.

check.stem: Why must the short parent in this cross be tt?

options.text: Shortness is recessive, so both alleles must be the recessive form
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
A single T allele makes the plant tall.

options.text: The short parent might be TT
options.explanation: TT plants are tall.
Genotype is inherited, not environmental.

check.stem: What offspring ratio does Tt crossed with tt give?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Half the cells receive tt.
That ratio needs two heterozygous parents.
The T gametes still exist.

check.stem: Which parental gametes decide the offspring's height here?

options.text: The heterozygous parent's T or t gametes decide it
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The short parent offers only t.
The grid is about alleles.
No mutation is involved.

check.stem: A tall offspring appears from this cross. What is its genotype?

options.text: Tt, the only tall genotype available in this grid
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The short parent cannot supply T.
That genotype is short.
Only one tall genotype is possible here.

check.stem: This pairing is often called a test cross. What is it testing?

options.text: Whether the tall parent carries a hidden t allele
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The shortness of the other parent
options.explanation: The short parent's genotype is already certain.
The cross is genetic, not agricultural.
Height is the trait under test.

check.stem: Set out the Tt by tt cross in words.
check.modelAnswer: The heterozygous parent gives T or t, the short parent gives t only, so the offspring are half Tt tall and half tt short.

check.stem: State the probability of a short offspring from Tt crossed with tt.
check.modelAnswer: The probability is one half, or 50 percent.

check.stem: Explain why no TT offspring can appear in this cross.
check.modelAnswer: The short parent carries no T allele to donate, so every offspring must receive t from that side and the dominant homozygote is impossible.

check.stem: A grower crosses an unknown tall plant with a short plant and gets half tall, half short offspring. What does the outcome reveal about the unknown parent, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The unknown tall parent must be heterozygous, because a homozygous tall parent could only have produced all tall offspring against the short partner.

lessons.title: From Ratio to Probability
sourceHeadings: Predicting Probabilities of Outcomes from Monohybrid Crosses
lessons.opening: The same grid converts directly into probabilities: with two heterozygous pea plants, three of the four cells carry the dominant phenotype, so any one offspring has a 75 percent chance of being tall and a 25 percent chance of being short.
keyPoints: Probabilities come from counting cells in the completed grid.
Tt crossed with Tt gives TT, two Tt and tt across four cells.
Three tall cells out of four means a 75 percent chance of tall.
The remaining cell means a 25 percent chance of short.

low.restatement: Count the tall boxes, divide by four, and that is your percentage.
low.analogy: A spinner with four equal sectors, three of them painted tall.
low.examPointer: Ratios describe the brood; percentages describe each single offspring.

medium.restatement: Each fertilisation is independent, so the percentage is a per-event chance, not a batch quota.
medium.analogy: Four coins tossed do not guarantee exactly three heads, though the chance per coin stays 75 percent in this analogy.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish ratio language from probability language in answers.

check.stem: From Tt crossed with Tt, what is the probability that one offspring is tall?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That figure belongs to the test cross.
25 percent is the short-offspring chance.
The recessive cell exists, so certainty fails.

check.stem: Where does the 75 percent figure come from?

options.text: Three of the four grid cells show the tall phenotype
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Parent phenotype does not set offspring probability.
The figure comes from the grid, not repetition.
Environment is outside the grid.

check.stem: Two heterozygotes produce four offspring. Must exactly three be tall?

options.text: No, each offspring is an independent 75 percent event
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Ratios are expectations, not promises.

options.text: No, because ratios are impossible to calculate
options.explanation: The ratio is exactly what the grid gives.
Independent events vary freely.

check.stem: What is the probability that a single offspring of Tt crossed with Tt is homozygous recessive?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That is the dominant phenotype chance.
Half would mean two recessive cells.
The tt cell exists in the grid.

check.stem: A grower wants mostly tall offspring from two tall plants of unknown genotype. What does the taught grid advise?

options.text: Check whether the parents are TT or Tt, since TT crossed with TT guarantees tall while Tt crossed with Tt risks short
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The grid offers a genetic answer.
Irrigation does not change genotypes.
That defeats the goal.

check.stem: Convert the 3:1 phenotypic ratio into percentages.
check.modelAnswer: Three tall cells out of four give 75 percent tall, and the single short cell gives 25 percent short.

check.stem: State the genotype ratio hidden behind the 3:1 phenotype ratio.
check.modelAnswer: It is one TT to two Tt to one tt.

check.stem: Explain why predictions from a Punnett square improve decisions in breeding programmes.
check.modelAnswer: The grid quantifies the chance of each phenotype before any cross is performed, so breeders can pick parental genotypes that maximise the trait they want.

check.stem: Two heterozygous pea plants are crossed and the grower plants exactly one seed. State the probability that this single plant is short.
check.modelAnswer: The probability is 25 percent, the one short cell out of the four, independent of what any sibling would have shown.

glossary.definition: A grid that pairs parental alleles to list every possible offspring genotype.
An inheritance pattern controlled by a single gene.
The first offspring generation from a cross between pure-breeding parents.
The generation produced by interbreeding the F1 offspring.
The count of phenotype classes among the offspring, such as 3:1.
